Deep learning · chapter 2.9 · transfer learning

Transfer Learning

Learn to see on one task, then reuse the eyes on another

Training a network from nothing takes a mountain of labelled examples. Usually you don't have one. But someone else, on some other task, may have trained a network whose early layers already know how to see: edges, strokes, curves, textures. Transfer learning keeps those layers and teaches only what is new. The network on this page learned to read 232,365 handwritten Japanese characters; it has never seen a digit. On the right, slide the number of labelled digits it is given, and compare it with the same network trained from scratch.

The idea
Keep the layers that learned to see; replace the layer that names things
Two recipes
Freeze the body and train a new head, or fine-tune everything gently
In practice
The default in vision, speech and language: almost nobody starts from random weights

The idea

Borrow a network that already sees

Split a trained classifier in two. The body turns pixels into a vector of features; the head, usually one layer, turns those features into class scores. The head is specific to the old task: it names 49 Japanese characters. The body is more general: its first layer detects tiny strokes and edges, and Yosinski and colleagues (2014) showed that such early features transfer from task to task, while the last layers become more and more specific to the task they were trained on. So we throw away the head, keep the body, and bolt on a new head with one output per digit. Below is the real body used throughout this chapter: two convolutional layers and a dense layer, trained in numpy on Kuzushiji-49. Show it a digit, a piece of clothing or a hiragana character and watch which features light up.

\[ \begin{aligned} f_{\text{new}}(\mathbf{x}) &= h_{\text{new}}\big(\varphi_{\text{pre}}(\mathbf{x})\big) \\ \varphi_{\text{pre}} &= \text{dense}\circ\text{pool}\circ\text{conv}_2 \\ &\qquad \circ\,\text{pool}\circ\text{conv}_1 \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: φ (phi) is the pretrained body: it maps a 14×14 image to 64 features. h is the head: a single layer, Wᵀφ + b, giving one score per class. Transfer learning reuses φ, which cost hundreds of thousands of labelled examples to learn, and trains a fresh h for the new task, which is cheap.
Say it“The new model is the new head applied to the pretrained features of x.”
features switched on (of 64)
the old head's guess
numbers in the body
numbers in a new 10-class head

Pretrained features

A better space to compare things in

Why would features learned on Japanese help with digits? Test it with the simplest classifier there is. Take n labelled digits of each class, average them into ten prototypes, and label every test digit by its nearest prototype. Do it in three spaces: the raw pixels, the features of the same network with random weights, and the pretrained features. The classifier is identical; only the space changes. Switch the space and change n. The scatter is the first two principal components of each space (chapter 1.13): a flat shadow of 64 or 196 dimensions, so judge by the accuracy, not only by the picture.

\[ \begin{aligned} \boldsymbol{\mu}_c &= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i:\,y_i=c} \varphi(\mathbf{x}_i) \\ \hat y(\mathbf{x}) &= \arg\min_c\ \big\Vert \varphi(\mathbf{x}) - \boldsymbol{\mu}_c \big\Vert^2 \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: the prototype μc of class c is the average feature vector of its n labelled examples. A new image gets the class of the closest prototype. Nothing is trained, so the accuracy measures the space itself: in a good space, images of the same class sit close together and far from the other classes.
Say it“Mu-c is the mean feature vector of class c; predict the class whose mean is nearest.”
nearest-prototype accuracy
% with pixels · random · pretrained

Recipe one

Freeze the body, train a head

Prototypes are a start, but a trained head can weight the features that matter. Freeze every weight of the body, compute each image's 64 features once, and fit a softmax regression (chapter 1.3) on top. This is a linear probe: cheap, convex, and impossible to wreck the body with. It is also how researchers measure how good a representation is. Train the head on pretrained features, then on raw pixels, with the same labelled digits. Watch the training accuracy race to 100% either way; only the test accuracy tells them apart.

\[ \begin{aligned} L &= -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i} \log p_{i,y_i} + \frac{\lambda}{2}\Vert W\Vert^2 \\ \mathbf{p}_i &= \operatorname{softmax}\!\big(W^{\top}\mathbf{z}_i + \mathbf{b}\big) \\ \nabla_{W} L &= \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i} \mathbf{z}_i\,(\mathbf{p}_i - \mathbf{e}_{y_i})^{\top} + \lambda W \\ \mathbf{z}_i &= \varphi_{\text{pre}}(\mathbf{x}_i) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: the usual cross-entropy, but the inputs are the frozen features zi, not the pixels. pi is the predicted probability vector (pi,yi its entry for the true class) and eyi the one-hot true label, so each gradient term is the feature vector times the prediction error. Nothing flows into φ: the body cannot change. λ is a small weight decay (10−3), the optimiser is full-batch Adam, 300 steps.
Say it“The loss is the average negative log-probability of the right class, computed from frozen features, plus lambda over two times W squared.”
training accuracy
test accuracy

Recipe two

Fine-tuning: let the body move, gently

A frozen body can only offer the features it already has. Fine-tuning starts from the pretrained weights and lets every layer keep learning on the new data. Two habits make it work. First, train the new head on its own before unfreezing (Kumar et al., 2022, call this LP-FT: linear probe, then fine-tune), so the body isn't hit by the large, random gradients of an untrained head. Second, give the body a small learning rate, so it adjusts its features instead of overwriting them. Push the body's learning rate too high and two things happen: the gain on the new task shrinks again, and the body forgets the hiragana it knew. We can measure the forgetting by reattaching the old head. Turn the body's learning rate and fine-tune.

\[ \begin{aligned} \theta_{\text{head}} &\leftarrow \theta_{\text{head}} - \eta\,\hat g_{\text{head}} \\ \theta_{\text{body}} &\leftarrow \theta_{\text{body}} - m\,\eta\,\hat g_{\text{body}} \\ \theta_{\text{body}}^{(0)} &= \theta_{\text{pre}} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: both parts take Adam steps (ĝ is Adam's normalised gradient, chapter 2.3), but the body's step is scaled by a multiplier m. m = 0 is the frozen probe; m = 1 is plain fine-tuning at the head's rate. Because the body starts at θpre and takes only 50 small steps, it stays close to where it began: a few steps, a small learning rate and weight decay act together as an implicit pull towards the pretrained solution. Li, Grandvalet & Davoine (2018) make that pull explicit with the penalty ½α‖θ − θpre‖² (“L2-SP”).
Say it“The head steps by eta times its Adam gradient; the body, which starts at the pretrained weights, steps by m times eta.”
digits (new task)
hiragana (old task)
how far the body moved
training accuracy

A dial, not a switch

How much to freeze?

Freezing and fine-tuning are the two ends of a dial. You can freeze the first layers (the most generic) and fine-tune the rest, unfreezing one more block as the data grows. Each block you free gives the model more ways to fit the new task, and more ways to overfit it. Below, four networks start from the same pretrained body and the same probe head, then train for the same 50 steps with different parts frozen. Pick n and train all four.

\[ \#\text{trainable}(k) = \sum_{\ell > k} \big(\,|W_\ell| + |\mathbf{b}_\ell|\,\big) \]
Read it as: freeze the first k layers and only the parameters above them learn. With 10 classes, that is 650 numbers for the head alone, 9,930 once the dense layer is free, 11,098 with the second convolution and all 11,178 when nothing is frozen. More free parameters means more capacity to adapt, and more need for data.
Say it“The number of trainable parameters is the total size of the weights and biases above the frozen layers.”
best setting
best minus frozen body

When transfer fails

Domain shift: how far is the new task?

Transfer works when the source and target look alike to the network. Digits and hiragana are both pen strokes on a blank background; clothes are photographs with texture and filled-in shapes. How do you measure “alike”? Ben-David and colleagues gave a neat answer: train a classifier to tell source images from target images using the features. If it can't, the domains look the same in feature space and a head trained on one will behave on the other; if it can, they are far apart. Rotate the digits, or switch to clothes, and compare the domain distance with what the pretrained features are actually worth on that target.

\[ \varepsilon_T(h) \le \varepsilon_S(h) + \tfrac12\, d_{\mathcal{H}\Delta\mathcal{H}}(S, T) + \lambda \]
Read it as: a classifier's error on the target domain T is at most its error on the source S, plus a term for how different the two domains are (as seen by the class of classifiers), plus λ, the error of the best single classifier for both. Transfer is safe when the middle term is small.
Say it“Target error is at most source error plus half the H-delta-H distance between the domains plus lambda.”
\[ \hat d_{\mathcal{A}} = 2\,(1 - 2\,\varepsilon_{\text{dom}}) \]
Read it as: the proxy A-distance. Label source features 0 and target features 1, train a logistic regression to separate them, and measure its held-out error εdom. A coin flip (ε = 0.5) gives 0: indistinguishable domains. Perfect separation (ε = 0) gives the maximum, 2.
Say it“The proxy A-distance is two times one minus twice the domain classifier's error.”
proxy A-distance to hiragana
gain over a pixel probe

The payoff

Small-data wins, and when they fade

Put the three recipes on one chart: test accuracy against the number of labelled examples, for every n we trained, averaged over five different random draws of the labelled examples (all computed in numpy; the project re-runs them in your browser). The useful way to read the gap is horizontally, in data: to reach a given accuracy, how many labelled examples does training from scratch need, compared with fine-tuning? Hernandez and colleagues (2021) call the difference the effective data transferred. Drag the accuracy you need.

\[ D_T = D_{\text{scratch}}(a) - D_{\text{fine-tune}}(a) \]
Read it as: D(a) is the number of labelled examples a method needs to reach accuracy a. Pretraining was worth DT labelled examples of the new task: that is what you would have had to collect, label and pay for to get the same model without it. The ratio Dscratch/Dfine-tune is the data multiplier.
Say it“Effective data transferred is the data scratch needs minus the data fine-tuning needs, at the same accuracy.”
scratch needs (per class)
fine-tuning needs
data multiplier
effective data transferred

Which recipe, when?

Target looks like the sourceTarget looks different
Few labelsFreeze the body, train a head; fine-tune gently if you can validate it. The biggest wins live here.The hard corner. Frozen features can hurt; fine-tune carefully, try earlier (more generic) layers, or find a closer source.
Many labelsFine-tune everything. Pretraining still speeds up training and usually adds a little accuracy.Fine-tune everything, or train from scratch: with enough data the head start matters less and less.
Real-world project

Project: reading digits with a network that learned Japanese

Kuzushiji-49 (Clanuwat et al., 2018) holds 270,912 images of 49 characters (48 hiragana and one iteration mark), handwritten in the cursive kuzushiji style and cut from pre-modern Japanese books digitised by the National Institute of Japanese Literature; 232,365 are for training. Our small CNN was trained on those offline in numpy (5 epochs of minibatch Adam; 77.5% accuracy on the 38,547 test images at our 14×14 resolution) and its weights are embedded in this page. The target is MNIST (LeCun et al., 1998), handwritten digits; for a far target, Fashion-MNIST (Xiao et al., 2017), photographs of clothes. All images are reduced to 14×14 pixels with 16 grey levels to keep the page small. For each n, your browser now trains three networks on n labelled examples per class: one from scratch (random weights, 150 Adam steps at learning rate 0.003), one frozen (pretrained body, new head, 300 steps) and one fine-tuned (start from the frozen one, then 50 gentle steps on everything). The same runs in numpy appear beside them.

Where the borrowed eyes help

After training, pick n and look at test images that the scratch network gets wrong but the fine-tuned network gets right, and the reverse.

The same experiment in numpy

import numpy as np   # tl-net.py: the CNN (im2col convolutions, average pooling) with fwd() and grads()
from tl_net import fwd, grads, acc, PRE, init_net, labelled   # PRE: the K49-pretrained weights, float32 -> float64

def adam(P, X, y, T, lr, wd, first):          # full-batch Adam; params with index >= first are trained
    P = [w.copy() for w in P]; m = [0 * w for w in P]; v = [0 * w for w in P]
    for t in range(1, T + 1):
        g, loss = grads(P, X, y, wd, first)
        for i in range(first, 8):
            m[i] = 0.9 * m[i] + 0.1 * g[i]; v[i] = 0.999 * v[i] + 0.001 * g[i] * g[i]
            P[i] = P[i] - lr * (m[i] / (1 - 0.9 ** t)) / (np.sqrt(v[i] / (1 - 0.999 ** t)) + 1e-8)
    return P

for target in ["digits", "clothes"]:
    for n in [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50]:
        res = []
        for draw in range(5):
            X, y, X_test, y_test = labelled(target, draw, n)                  # n labelled images per class
            frozen = adam(PRE[:6] + [np.zeros((64, 10)), np.zeros(10)], X, y, 300, 0.01, 1e-3, first=6)
            tuned = adam(frozen, X, y, 50, 1e-3, 1e-3, first=0)               # LP-FT: probe, then everything
            scratch = adam(init_net(seed=7, K=10), X, y, 150, 3e-3, 1e-3, first=0)
            res.append([acc(P, X_test, y_test) for P in (scratch, frozen, tuned)])
        r = np.array(res)
        print(f"{target:7s} n={n:2d}  draw 1: " + " ".join(f"{a:.4f}" for a in r[0]) +
              "   mean of 5: " + " ".join(f"{a:.3f}±{s:.3f}" for a, s in zip(r.mean(0), r.std(0))))
digits  n= 1  draw 1: 0.4335 0.5665 0.5535   mean of 5: 0.456±0.017 0.584±0.041 0.586±0.044
digits  n= 2  draw 1: 0.5560 0.6650 0.6705   mean of 5: 0.562±0.045 0.674±0.038 0.684±0.050
digits  n= 5  draw 1: 0.7145 0.8110 0.8220   mean of 5: 0.717±0.017 0.825±0.010 0.834±0.009

The browser and numpy start from identical weights (the scratch initialisation comes from the same mulberry32 generator, ported to Python), see identical images and take identical Adam steps in double precision. The only differences are the order in which floating-point sums are added, so final losses agree to about 10−10 and every accuracy above matches to the image. Honest caveats: the images are 14×14 and the network is tiny, so all accuracies are lower than full-size models reach; the hyperparameters (steps, learning rates) were fixed in advance for every n rather than tuned per n, because with one labelled example per class there is nothing left to validate on; and a different scratch initialisation would move the small-n scratch numbers by a few points.

Wrap-up

Five lines to remember

  • A trained network is a body that turns inputs into features and a head that names classes. Transfer learning keeps the body, f = hnew(φpre(x)), and trains a new head.
  • Early layers learn generic patterns (edges, strokes); later layers become specific to the task they were trained on. That is why bodies travel and heads don't.
  • Freezing the body (a linear probe) is cheap and safe; fine-tuning, after the head is trained and with a small body learning rate, adapts the features and usually wins, but can overfit and forget.
  • Transfer helps in proportion to how alike the domains are: hiragana features were worth about 13 points on digits with five labels per class, but only a few on clothes, and nothing by 50. Distance measures such as the proxy A-distance flag a shift; only a baseline on the target tells you whether the features help.
  • The gains are largest when labels are scarce, and measured in data they are large: to reach 80% on digits, fine-tuning needed about 4 labelled examples per class and scratch about 11. With enough data, scratch catches up.

Check your understanding

Why replace the head instead of reusing it?

The old head maps features to the old classes (49 hiragana). The new task has different classes, ten digits, so it needs a new output layer with one score per new class. Only the body's features are meant to be shared.

Why train the new head first, before unfreezing the body?

A freshly initialised head produces large, essentially random errors, and their gradients flow straight into the pretrained body and scramble its features in the first steps. Training the head on frozen features first (LP-FT) means fine-tuning starts from sensible predictions and small, meaningful gradients.

You have 50,000 labelled X-ray images and an ImageNet-pretrained network. Freeze or fine-tune?

Fine-tune, probably all of it: X-rays look quite different from everyday photos, and 50,000 images are enough to adapt every layer without overfitting badly. Pretraining still gives a better starting point and faster training than random weights.

The domain classifier separates your source and target features with 99% accuracy. What do you expect?

A proxy A-distance close to 2: the domains are easy to tell apart. That is a warning, not a verdict; on this page upright digits score about 1.8 and still gain 10 points from the hiragana features. Compare the frozen-feature head with a baseline (pixels, or a scratch model) on held-out target data; if it loses, fine-tune more of the network, use earlier layers, or find a source closer to your data.

After fine-tuning with a large learning rate, the network's accuracy on the original task collapses. What is this called, and why might you care?

Catastrophic forgetting: the shared weights were rewritten for the new task. You care if the model must still do the old task, or if the old knowledge was what made the new task work; a smaller body learning rate, fewer steps or an L2-SP penalty all limit it.
